By

Jill Terreri Ramos 
  

October 28, 2020

# Jacob’s charge that McMurray raised taxes on Grand Island is correct

In a rematch between Rep. Chris Jacobs, a Republican, and Democrat Nate McMurray for the 27th Congressional District seat, Jacobs says his opponent has a track record of raising taxes and a desire to do so again.

In a large postcard sent to voters, the Jacobs campaign links McMurray with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of Queens and says: “Nate McMurray Big Tax, Big Spend: An AOC Progressive Who Will Raise Taxes.”

The mailer claims that “While serving as Town Supervisor, Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.”

We were curious about McMurray’s record on Grand Island, where he served as supervisor for four years, beginning in 2016.

## Slight increases

We spoke with McMurray, who confirmed that as a member of the town board on Grand Island, he voted to slightly increase taxes. He also proposed budgets, as supervisor, with slight tax increases, he said.

During all four years of his tenure, the increases remained under the property tax cap, he said. He also said that he was one of five people on the board, where Republicans held the other four seats.

“I had no control to raise taxes myself,” he said.

Taxes increased about $27 in 2018 for a house assessed at $210,600. The tax rate for the general fund, which makes up a large amount of town spending, decreased by 3.1%, but an increase in the sewer district tax led to the increase. The 20% of residents without sewer access generally did not have an increase.

The town’s official meeting minutes of the board session with the budget vote show that McMurray voted in favor of the increase.

McMurray said he sometimes had to fight to keep the increases from getting too high during negotiations with other board members. “I’m one of five, and everybody has their pet thing.”

In the 2019 budget, adopted in late 2018, the tax levy, or the amount raised in taxes, increased by 28% on Grand Island for the sewer system fund, though overall levy increase was 2.63 percent. Rates increased only for people using the sewer system and went down for those who do not. The combined levy for the general and highway funds fell by 4%. McMurray voted in favor of this budget.

The town’s sewer system needed costly repairs, and a prior administration reached a deal with the state Department of Environmental Conservation, McMurray said. It was his administration’s obligation to fund them, he said, a statement supported by a 2017 outside auditor’s report.

The general fund tax rate was lower when he left office than it was during his first year, but that is not true of all of the funds that tax residents.

McMurray said that the mailer makes it seem like he was recklessly raising taxes as supervisor. “It’s acting like we’re willy-nilly raising taxes,” he said. “Sure, there was a moderate increase under the tax cap.”

McMurray has campaigned on his fiscal management of Grand Island, including a claim from 2018, in which he said he was a “small-town supervisor who has kept a balanced budget, who has increased surpluses, who has led us to the highest credit rating our town has ever had.” PolitiFact rated that claim True.

## Our ruling

Jacobs said McMurray

# Erie County’s proposed 2027 budget increases spending 5.5%

BY 

Hunter Caparelli
Buffalo

PUBLISHED 5:51 PM ET Oct. 15, 2026
PUBLISHED 5:51 PM EDT Oct. 15, 2026

SHARE

BUFFALO, N.Y. — Erie County’s proposed 2027 budget calls for a 5.5% increase in spending, about $125 million more than this year. County Executive Mark Poloncarz said rising costs are driving that increase, while critics are questioning whether taxpayers are getting enough relief.

Erie County's proposed budget tops $2.2 billion in general fund spending. Poloncarz said the county is trying to balance rising costs with the need to keep taxes in check.

“The 2027 budget is very tight," said Poloncarz. "It's a balanced budget. It's a fair budget. It doesn't have any bells and whistles.”

The proposal includes a $12.7 million increase in the property tax levy, but the county said the property tax rate will drop from $3.9 to $3.1 per $1,000 of assessed value. Poloncarz said that doesn't guarantee every homeowner will pay less.

“If somebody’s assessment stayed the same when it comes to their county taxes, they will see a reduction in what they paid last year," said Poloncarz. "If their assessment went up, they could theoretically pay more. We reduced the rate and that’s all we can control.”

Director of the Office of Budget and Management Mark Cornell said the budget also includes $42 million in spending cuts, after departments requested even more funding.

“All of the benefit that the county gets from sales tax is going right back into dollars out the door to pay for the cost also associated with inflation and higher costs," said Cornell.

The county said its budget stays within the state tax cap, but officials warn future federal and state costs could put more pressure on county finances. The county legislature is expected to review the proposal in the coming weeks. Erie County lawmakers are expected to hold budget hearings in November, with action on the proposed budget expected in early December.

# POLONCARZ UNVEILS 2027 PROPOSED ERIE COUNTY BUDGET

Thursday, October 15, 2026

Erie County Executive Mark C. Poloncarz was joined today by Director of the Erie County Office of Budget and Management Mark Cornell to unveil the 2027 Proposed Erie County Budget (“the Budget”). Balanced and fiscally prudent, the 2027 Proposed Budget is $2.408 billion for all Operating Funds. While the county’s Property Tax Levy has grown by 3.6% or $12.7 million, the county’s Property Tax Rate will reduce from the current $3.09 per thousand dollars of assessed value to $3.01, a reduction of $0.08, which stays under the NYS Tax Cap and once again gives Erie County the lowest property tax rate by far of any of the eight WNY counties. The Poloncarz administration has decreased the county’s Property Tax Rate by 40.2%, or $2.02 per thousand, since 2012. 

“The 2027 Budget is very tight, with no new programs or services except for the expected opening of Willowdale Park in 2027. This Budget funds the necessary and mandated programs that are critical to our community but is also cognizant of the burdens and obstacles that are coming because of congressional actions,” **said Erie County Executive Mark C. Poloncarz.** “The ‘One Big Beautiful Bill Act’ that congressional republicans are now trying to hide from after voting for it is really ‘The Big Shift’ because it is shifting service costs from the Federal Government down to State & Local Governments. The Big Shift is already having an impact on us.”

Poloncarz pointed to changes in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (“SNAP”) as harbingers of the damage that the Big Shift will do to communities like Erie County. Effective October 1st of this year, a 25% cut to SNAP administration reimbursement took place; while the program was funded 50/50 between the federal government and the county prior to the change, it is now 25% federal and 75% county. This results in a $10.2 million loss in revenue for 2027. The Big Shift also passes along a 50% increase in employment and training costs for the program, which increases the county’s share by $3.6 million. The county must provide the service, which means the county must fund this $13.8 million expense from local dollars. 

Effective October 1st of 2027 (without congressional action), there will be a 15% increase in SNAP benefits’ cost; assuming this new cost is passed on to the counties by the state, this will add approximately $55 million annually to the county’s burden. The Big Shift also forces seniors to continue to work until age 64 to maintain eligibility, removes exemptions for working families by reducing dependent child age from under 18 to 7, and eliminates the Standard Utility Allowance for working households.

“The SNAP program is, for many families and individuals, the last line of defense before going hungry. It is what helps working families to get food on the table for their children, it is what allows older adults on fixed incomes to have some dignity in their nutritional choices, and it is an essential tool in the fight against hunger,” **said Poloncarz.** “However, for congressional republicans, giving unneeded tax breaks to billionaires was more important than ensuring that hungry Americans had access to food.”

Poloncarz also noted cuts and changes to Medicaid that are included in the Big Shift.  Changes to program eligibility will purge an estimated 1.2 – 1.5 million NY residents from Medicaid, including 5,000 -10,000 Erie County residents.
As previously announced, my 2027 proposed Erie County, NY Budget will reduce the county's tax rate by 8 cents per thousand: from $3.09 to $3.01.
